analysis.summary:
This 32-year-old male presents with a pattern that is classic for Heart Blood and Yin deficiency precipitated by acute sleep deprivation. Two months of staying up late have exhausted his Kidney Yin essence and Heart Blood, creating a foundation for all his current symptoms. The weak and deep pulse directly indicates both Qi and Blood deficiency; the Heart cannot pump effectively and cannot hold enough blood to adequately nourish consciousness. The red puffy tongue with cracks and yellow fur reveals both heat (from Yin deficiency allowing relative heat to accumulate) and fluid depletion (cracks indicate dryness). His insomnia and palpitations are the Shen (consciousness/spirit) losing its anchor—without adequate Blood and Yin, the Shen becomes agitated and restless, preventing sleep and causing the heart to race erratically.

The constipation that developed later is a secondary manifestation: depleted Yin and Blood mean less fluid to moisten the intestines, and the heat trapped from Yin deficiency can dry out the bowels further. All of these signs fit together coherently and point to a single underlying mechanism: Yin and Blood depletion from sleep deprivation, allowing relative heat accumulation and failing to anchor consciousness.

Constitutionally, this patient is clearly Yin-deficient. His prior health (evidenced by the fact that he maintained late hours for two months without prior cardiac issues) suggests he was previously closer to balanced, but the acute insult of prolonged sleep loss has pushed him into manifest deficiency. This is important because it means his condition is not deeply entrenched and can respond well to treatment that rebuilds Yin and Blood while calming the Shen and clearing the excess heat.

From the pulse perspective, the weakness indicates inadequate Heart Qi to pump effectively, while the deep quality suggests the body is pulling Qi inward due to deficiency (a protective mechanism when reserves are low). Neither indicates an exterior pathogen or acute excess condition; this is clearly a deficiency pattern requiring tonification, not purging.

The prognosis is good if treatment is started promptly and the patient commits to sleep schedule reform. The deficiency is the result of acute stress (sleep loss) rather than a chronic constitutional weakness that developed over years.

Black sesame seeds — Sweet, neutral, enters Liver and Kidney. Richly nourishes Blood and Yin; particularly effective for the dryness and constipation from Yin deficiency. Toast and grind into powder, 1 tablespoon daily in congee or milk.
recipes: Heart-Blood Tonifying Congee: 50g white rice, 10 red dates (pitted), 6-8 goji berries, 1 small piece of dried angelica root (if available), 800ml water. Simmer rice until very soft (45 minutes), add dates and goji in the last 10 minutes. Eat warm every morning for 2-3 weeks. This recipe directly addresses Heart Blood deficiency and insomnia.

Yin-Nourishing Sweet Soup: 15-20 lotus seeds, 6-8 red dates (pitted), 10g white fungus (soaked), 500ml water, 2 tbsp honey or rock sugar. Simmer all ingredients 45 minutes until very soft, add honey at the end. Drink as an evening snack 3-4 times per week. Settles Shen and moistens dryness.

Spleen-Supporting Pork Bone Broth: 200g lean pork or pork bones, 6 red dates, 6-8 dried shiitake mushrooms, 1 dried astragalus root (if available), 1000ml water. Simmer 90 minutes. Drink the broth, eat the pork. This rebuilds Qi and Blood for circulation.

foods_to_avoid: Spicy foods (chili, black pepper, ginger if heated) — Consume the remaining Yin fluid and exacerbate internal heat, worsening palpitations and insomnia. Avoid all chili-based dishes and overly warming spices.

Fried and greasy foods (deep-fried pastries, fatty meats, oil-heavy dishes) — Damage Spleen function, impede circulation of Blood and Qi (making palpitations worse), and consume Yin fluid through heat damage. Avoid fried snacks, greasy take-out, and butter-heavy foods.

Caffeine (coffee, strong black tea, energy drinks, chocolate) — Stimulates Heart fire and interferes with Yin. Directly worsens palpitations and makes insomnia much worse. Avoid entirely until symptoms resolve (at least 4-6 weeks).
Alcohol (all spirits and strong wines) — Burns Yin fluid directly and agitates the Shen. Even small amounts will worsen sleep and palpitations. Avoid completely during treatment.

Cold or raw foods (ice cream, ice water, raw salads, uncooked vegetables) — Cold directly damages Spleen Yang (needed to digest and extract Blood), slows circulation, and weakens the digestive fire needed to turn food into nourishing Blood. All foods and beverages should be warm or room-temperature.
lifestyle: Sleep schedule reform (CRITICAL): Establish a consistent bedtime of 10:00-11:00 PM and wake time of 6:00-7:00 AM. Sleep 7-8 hours nightly, every single night. Irregular sleep perpetuates Yin depletion. This is the single most important intervention—without sleep recovery, no herbal formula will fully work. Treat this as non-negotiable medical treatment.

Evening wind-down routine (30-45 minutes before bed): Stop all work, close the laptop, dim lights. Do gentle abdominal breathing (breathe in slowly for 4 counts through the nose, hold 4 counts, exhale slowly for 4 counts through the mouth) 10-20 breaths. Listen to soft instrumental music or nature sounds. Avoid all screens (blue light stimulates Heart fire). Never do work emails or watch news before bed. A calm evening mind allows Yin to settle and Shen to anchor.

Temperature and hydration: Drink warm water throughout the day (never cold or ice water). Eat all foods warm or at room temperature. Keep the environment moderately warm, not hot or cold. Wrap the lower back lightly (Kidney Yin originates here). These maintain Spleen function and prevent additional Yin damage.

Limit physical exertion (first 2 weeks in particular): Rest is essential when Qi and Blood are low. Do not exercise intensely, run long distances, or lift heavy weights. Gentle movement only (see Exercise section). Overexertion consumes Qi faster than the body can rebuild it from rest and food, perpetuating the deficit.
acupoints: Shenmen (Heart 7) — Located on the wrist crease on the pinky-side of the transverse wrist crease, in the depression at the ulnar end where the radial artery pulses (medial to the wrist crease, in line with the pinky finger). Using the thumb or index finger, apply firm steady pressure in small circular motions for 1-2 minutes, breathing deeply; massage toward the elbow (not toward fingers). This is the master point for calming the Spirit and stopping palpitations; use daily, ideally in the evening or whenever palpitations occur.

Neiguan (Pericardium 6) — Located on the inner forearm, 2 cun (approximately 2 finger-widths) above the wrist crease, directly between the two forearm tendons (on the line running from the middle finger down the center of the forearm). Press with the thumb and massage gently in circular motions for 1-2 minutes, 1-2 times daily. This point regulates Heart rhythm, reduces anxiety, and is especially helpful for palpitations and shallow breathing.

Sanyinjiao (Spleen 6) — Located on the inner leg, 3 cun above the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus, the bony bump on the inside of the ankle), in the groove between the tibia (shin bone) and fibula (smaller calf bone). Massage gently with the thumb in circular motions for 2-3 minutes, 1-2 times daily (both legs). This point is central to nourishing Blood and Yin throughout the body and is particularly calming for insomnia and constipation.

Anmian (Peaceful Sleep) — Located in the depression directly behind the earlobe, between the lower edge of the earlobe and the bone. Massage gently with the thumb or index finger in circular motions for 1-2 minutes before sleep. This point specifically promotes sleep and calms the Shen when used before bedtime.
exercise: Tai Chi: Practice a simple form like the 8-movement or 24-movement form for 15-20 minutes each morning (ideally 6:00-8:00 AM when Yang is rising but moderate). Tai Chi gently moves Qi without depleting reserves, calms the mind, and is particularly beneficial for Heart palpitations and insomnia. Start with slow, flowing movements. Practice 5-6 days per week. Do not do vigorous martial Tai Chi styles; gentle classical styles only.

Gentle evening walking: After dinner, take a slow 20-30 minute walk at an easy pace (you should be able to speak in complete sentences). Walking aids digestion and gently moves Qi without overexertion. This is ideal 1-2 hours after eating. Avoid walking in strong wind or extreme heat. Do this 5-6 days per week.

Abdominal breathing: Sit or lie comfortably. Breathe in slowly through the nose for 4 counts, letting the abdomen expand (not the chest). Hold for 4 counts. Exhale slowly through the mouth for 4 counts, letting the abdomen relax. Repeat 20-40 breaths, 1-2 times daily, especially before sleep. This calms the Shen, regulates Heart rate, and activates the parasympathetic nervous system (rest-and-digest), supporting sleep.
recommendations.emotional_care: The two-month sleep deprivation has injured not only the Heart's physical Blood and Yin reserves, but also its spiritual-psychological anchor—consciousness (Shen) without a secure seat becomes anxious, scattered, and agitated, perpetuating insomnia. As you rebuild Blood and Yin with food and herbs, you must simultaneously calm the disturbed Shen through three practices: (1) Regulate sleep: your brain's neurochemical recovery depends on consistent sleep; every night of good sleep is neuro-repair. (2) Reduce mental stimulation: for the next 4 weeks, actively avoid stressful work, contentious relationships, stimulating entertainment, and news. If worries arise, write them down and set them aside—do not ruminate. (3) Cultivate quiet: spend 10-15 minutes daily in calm solitude, practicing the abdominal breathing, sitting by a window, or listening to water sounds. These simple acts retrain the nervous system that your body is safe to rest. Over 2-3 weeks, as sleep improves and Yin accumulates, anxiety and palpitations will naturally diminish. You are not broken—you are depleted. Depletion repairs with rest, nourishment, and time.

herbal_formulas.name: Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan (Emperor of Heaven's Special Pill to Tonify the Heart)
herbal_formulas.dosage: Classical formula available as patent pill or granule. If granules: 6-9 grams twice daily in warm water. If pills: follow manufacturer label (typically 8 pills 2-3 times daily). Take for 4-6 weeks minimum.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This is the classic formula for Heart Blood and Yin deficiency with insomnia and palpitations caused by stress or sleep loss. It directly nourishes Heart Blood and Yin, calms the Spirit, clears deficiency-heat, and is specifically designed to resolve this exact pattern. Among all available herbal formulas, this is the gold standard for your presentation.

herbal_formulas.name: Suan Zao Ren Tang (Zizyphus Spinosa Decoction)
herbal_formulas.dosage: If taking as a prepared granule or powder: dissolve 6-9g in warm water and drink 2 times daily. If decocting raw herbs: simmer all ingredients in 3 cups water for 30 minutes, strain, drink the liquid in 2 divided doses daily. Take for 2-4 weeks.
herbal_formulas.purpose: An alternative to Tian Wang, this formula is lighter and more suitable if you find Tian Wang too cloying or if Spleen digestion is weak. It nourishes Heart Blood, calms the Shen, and is particularly good for insomnia with emotional disturbance. Use this if you want a simpler formula or have poor digestion.

warning_signs: Severe chest pain or pressure (particularly radiating to left arm or shoulder) — seek emergency medical care immediately to exclude acute cardiac events such as myocardial infarction or angina

Sudden rapid heart rate that does not return to normal with rest (sustained tachycardia above 120 beats per minute) — may indicate thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism) or cardiac arrhythmia requiring medical evaluation
Fainting, loss of consciousness, or severe dizziness upon standing — suggests compromised cerebral perfusion or cardiac output requiring emergency evaluation
Shortness of breath at rest or with minimal exertion that worsens acutely — may indicate pulmonary or cardiac pathology requiring immediate medical care
Persistent vomiting or complete inability to eat for more than 24 hours — sign of worsening Spleen function and malnutrition requiring medical attention
No improvement or worsening of insomnia after 3-4 weeks of treatment despite perfect sleep hygiene — may indicate undiagnosed sleep apnea or other sleep disorder requiring sleep study evaluation
contraindications: Do NOT take stimulant medications or herbal stimulants (ephedrine-containing herbs, concentrated caffeine, guarana) — these directly counter the Yin-nourishing treatment and will worsen the condition
Do NOT fast or attempt severe calorie restriction — your body needs adequate nutrition to rebuild Blood and Yin from food; undereating perpetuates deficiency

Do NOT engage in intense endurance exercise (long-distance running, heavy weight lifting, high-intensity interval training) during treatment — this consumes Qi faster than it can be rebuilt and worsens exhaustion
Do NOT use stimulating entertainment near bedtime (violent movies, competitive video games, work stress) — this agitates the Shen and sabotages sleep recovery
Do NOT expose yourself to extreme heat or intense sun exposure without protection — heat depletes Yin fluid; keep cool and hydrated
Do NOT use herbal formulas containing stimulating warming herbs (dry ginger, cinnamon bark) in large amounts — these consume remaining Yin and exacerbate heat symptoms
precautions.special_notes: This condition—Heart Blood and Yin deficiency triggered by acute sleep deprivation—is highly responsive to combined treatment (herbal medicine plus sleep reform plus dietary therapy plus acupressure plus lifestyle change). However, the patient must understand that recovery is a process: Yin and Blood rebuild slowly over 4-8 weeks, not days. Symptoms like palpitations and insomnia typically begin to improve within 7-14 days of consistent treatment, but full resolution requires 4-6 weeks minimum. Do not abandon treatment early. Additionally, the bradycardia (slow heart rate) discovered at checkup is consistent with Heart Qi deficiency; as Heart Qi and Blood are rebuilt, heart rate should normalize on its own. If bradycardia persists or worsens after 4 weeks of treatment, inform your physician to rule out structural cardiac problems (conduction abnormality, valve dysfunction). Lastly, any future episodes of sleep deprivation will rapidly re-trigger symptoms in this constitution; once recovered, prioritize sleep as a foundational pillar of long-term health. The fact that this condition emerged from acute sleep loss (not chronic disease) means you likely have good recovery potential if you commit to the treatment plan.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess at 2 weeks (check for initial sleep improvement and reduction in palpitation frequency). Full reassessment at 4 weeks (tongue color, pulse quality, energy level, sleep quality, bowel function). Expect maximal improvement by 6-8 weeks.
follow_up.expected_improvement: At 1-2 weeks: Sleep onset latency decreases (falling asleep becomes easier), palpitations occur less frequently or with lower intensity, constipation begins to ease. At 3-4 weeks: Sleep quality improves (fewer nighttime awakenings, deeper sleep), palpitations rare, anxiety diminishes, energy improves, appetite normalizes, constipation resolved. At 6-8 weeks: Normal sleep restored, no palpitations, resting heart rate normalizes, mood stable, energy sustained, tongue color and coating return to normal, pulse becomes fuller and more forceful.
follow_up.next_steps: If 50% improvement is not evident by 4 weeks: Schedule consultation with a TCM practitioner who can adjust the herbal formula or add acupuncture (needle therapy is more powerful than acupressure). If symptoms worsen despite full adherence: Report to your physician to exclude hyperthyroidism, sleep apnea, cardiac arrhythmia, or other medical conditions that can mimic Heart Yin deficiency. Long-term after recovery: Maintain sleep schedule permanently (7-8 hours nightly), continue Tai Chi and abdominal breathing 3-4 times per week as preventive maintenance, and eat Heart-and-Yin-nourishing foods seasonally. This will prevent relapse and build constitutional resilience. One month post-recovery, you may taper herbal formulas if symptoms are completely resolved, but maintain dietary therapy and lifestyle practices indefinitely.

parsed.disclaimer: This Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnosis and recommendations are complementary to, not a replacement for, conventional medical care. A slow heart rate (bradycardia) and palpitations can occasionally indicate underlying cardiac, endocrine (thyroid), or neurological conditions that require medical evaluation. Before beginning this TCM treatment, please ensure your physician has evaluated you for cardiac arrhythmias, thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism), anemia, electrolyte imbalances, and sleep apnea. TCM works best as an integrated approach alongside conventional medicine. If symptoms worsen, do not improve within 4 weeks despite full adherence, or if you develop new symptoms (chest pain, fainting, rapid uncontrolled heart rate), contact your physician or emergency services immediately. This diagnosis was made from remote consultation without physical examination and direct pulse-taking; an in-person TCM consultation can refine the pattern further and may suggest additional or modified recommendations. The recommendations provided are evidence-based on classical TCM texts and modern clinical experience, but individual response varies. You are responsible for your own health decisions and medical safety.
